did_you_know.text: The LORD commands Jeremiah to buy a linen loincloth, wear it, and not put it in water. The linen emphasizes that this is an actual item of clothing, intended later to serve as a prophetic symbol.

After Jeremiah hides the loincloth and finds it many days later, he discovers that it is ruined and no longer fit for use. Its condition illustrates the corruption of the people addressed by the prophecy.

The LORD compares Israel and Judah to a loincloth worn close to a person’s waist: just as the loincloth is close to the body, so the LORD brought his people close to himself so that they would be his people, for renown, praise, and glory.

The illustration of the wine jars initially works like a simple riddle: every jar is indeed filled with wine. But the LORD uses the people’s answer to announce that the land and its inhabitants will be filled with drunkenness and confusion.

The drunkenness described in the chapter is not merely a personal condition but a picture of social and political disintegration: people will smash against one another, and conflict will even prevail within families.
The call, “Listen and pay attention; do not be proud,” connects listening to the LORD with giving up pride. According to the chapter, pride is an obstacle to accepting the word of the LORD.

Jeremiah describes weeping in secret over the captivity of “the LORD’s flock.” The image presents the people as a flock belonging to the LORD and expresses the prophet’s grief over the consequences of failing to listen.

The king and the queen mother are called to humble themselves because the crown of their glory has fallen. In this way, the chapter emphasizes that even those of the highest status are not exempt from responsibility and judgment.

The images of a Cushite’s skin and a leopard’s spots illustrate how deeply the habit of sin has become rooted: according to the comparison, those who have learned to do evil find it difficult to change their ways by their own efforts.

At the end of the chapter, Jerusalem is portrayed as unclean because her sins include cultic prostitution and loyalty to other gods. The closing words, “How long will it be?” leave the rebuke as a painful question about how long this behavior will continue.
